entry.title: Tracybot: Preserving Developer Intent by Tracing Agent-Generated Code to Prompts
entry.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are now widely used in software development, and LLM-based coding agents are given increasing autonomy. With coding agents, many design decisions are made in the conversation between the developer and the agent. Typically, the developer starts a conversation with an agent and states their intent, the agent proposes options if needed, and the developer plans the change accordingly. Then, the resulting code is committed. However, in such scenarios, the decisions and the intent behind the changes remain in the conversation, with no link to the code they produced. In this paper, we present Tracybot, an open-source tool that integrates with VS Code, Git, and coding agents to keep track of relevant conversations in an LLM-assisted development process. Tracybot captures each change as a Tasklet which consists of optional planning prompts used to plan a change, together with a build prompt that produces it. Tracybot has two main features: (i) it maps line-level code changes made by coding agents to the Tasklets that produced them, and (ii) it allows the developer to export a Tasklet as a decision record when needed, for example when the decision concerns the architecture of the project. We developed the tool over two iterations of a design science study, while focusing the evaluation on the usability and user-friendliness of the tool. In a focus group (7 participants) and a survey (24 participants), we found that Tracybot was perceived as useful for activities like code review, and most participants found our Tasklet design and presentation to be a clear way to represent the developer's intent. Tool: https://github.com/TracyTeam/tracybot. Video: https://youtu.be/Vg_a1F5eO04.

entry.title: Navigating Complexity: A User-Centered Evaluation of Project Management Tools
entry.summary: In the age of digital transformation, companies are increasingly relying on specialized software to manage the complexity of projects. However, when selecting tools, features and costs often take precedence over user experience (UX), leading to low adoption rates, user frustration, and project delays. This study empirically evaluates the user experience of leading project management tools (Jira, Trello, Monday.com, Asana, and Microsoft Project) across various project scales using a mixed methods approach. The System Usability Scale (SUS) was used as the primary quantitative instrument, with data collected from 141 experienced professionals via online questionnaires. The results reveal a significant trade-off between functionality and usability. Trello achieved the highest SUS score (77.5), indicating a superior user experience for small projects and agile teams, while Microsoft Project scored the lowest (51.2), suggesting significant usability challenges despite its robust features. Jira demonstrated a balanced profile, offering powerful features with manageable complexity. Statistical analyses confirmed that the choice of the optimal tool is highly context dependent, with team size and project complexity influencing UX outcomes. The findings underscore that UX is not a secondary feature but a critical success factor for software acceptance and project effectiveness. This study provides an evidence-based framework for aligning tool selection with the project context, offers practitioners actionable insights, and identifies design opportunities for software developers.

entry.title: Technohybridism: Recursive Semantic Normalization in AI-Mediated Societies
entry.summary: Language-generating AI systems are no longer only objects of linguistic interaction: their outputs increasingly re-enter the communicative and institutional practices from which their training material was drawn. Drawing on social theory, social epistemology, and the philosophy of language, this article develops a sociotechnical account of that re-entry. We introduce recursive semantic normalization: the process through which machine-generated formulations, once recurrently taken up, evaluated, reused, and institutionally retained, participate in the reproduction and transformation of semantic regularities. Under the heading of technohybridism, we argue that the relevant unit of analysis is the hybrid semantic system, a recursively coupled configuration of human practices, computational generation, and institutional uptake. First, we distinguish the concept from neighbouring accounts, including model collapse, looping effects, machine habitus, machine culture, and the epistemology of AI testimony. Second, we develop an analytical model that separates generation, selection, uptake, and persistence and distinguishes machine-attributable change from change that would have occurred anyway. Third, we analyse uptake as routinized, institutionally diffused, and socially stratified practice and state conditions under which machine-derived regularities become norms. Fourth, we identify social-epistemic consequences: the laundering of provenance that weakens epistemic vigilance, the erosion of the cognitive diversity on which collective inquiry depends, and the narrowing of shared hermeneutical resources. An evidential ladder for empirical research follows. The account attributes no normative authority to machine outputs; what changes is the field within which human and institutional uptake operates.

entry.title: STAG-Net: Structure-Aware Attention over Landmark Groups for Lightweight Head Pose Estimation
entry.summary: Head pose estimation is important for human computer interaction and driver monitoring, but many image based methods remain too costly for resource constrained deployment. We propose STAG-Net, a structure-aware attention over landmark groups for lightweight head Pose estimation that estimates head pose from facial landmarks using movement aware selection, spatial clustering, compact DeepSet encoders, self attention, and a global geometry descriptor. We develop variants using FaceMesh and Face Alignment Network landmarks and evaluate them under cross dataset and subject independent protocols on 300W-LP, AFLW2000, and BIWI. STAG-Net achieves the lowest mean absolute error among all compared landmark based methods in every evaluated setting. On BIWI frames with valid detections, the FAN variant also records the lowest overall error among all compared methods, reaching $3.51^\circ$ under cross dataset evaluation and $2.39^\circ$ under subject independent evaluation. The regressors use only 0.012 to 0.043 million parameters and 24.1 to 83.6 thousand FLOPs, about three orders of magnitude fewer FLOPs than FSA-Net. Despite including landmark extraction and regression, the FaceMesh pipeline reaches 322.9 frames per second on a Tesla T4 GPU, nearly twice the 164.5 frames per second of the fastest measured image based baseline, and 111.0 frames per second on CPU. After normalization by dataset size, STAG-Net processes training samples seven to eight times faster than FSA-Net and more than one hundred times faster than HopeNet and TokenHPE, while complete training finishes within 28 minutes. These results show that STAG-Net combines leading landmark based accuracy with substantially lower training and inference cost.

entry.title: ReviewMap: Mapping Evaluative Acts and Automation Boundaries in Peer-Review Comments
entry.summary: Peer-review comments check what a paper does and judge why it matters, but no existing scheme distinguishes these two evaluative acts. We argue that making these acts explicit and measuring how reliably LLMs identify them is a prerequisite for responsible LLM-assisted review analysis: humans need to inspect review judgments and their grounds. This defines a more honest mission for NLP in peer review than full automation. We present ReviewMap, a framework that classifies each comment as assessment of claims and scholarly standards or calibration of contribution value and venue fit, with finer-grained attributes applied conditionally by act type. Applied to 500 ICLR~2026 papers through multi-model LLM consensus, the act layer proves reliably automatable under the operational guideline (inter-model $κ\geq 0.75$), supported by five-human validation on 470 development comments, while the attribute layer requires human oversight, defining a measured automation boundary. At the corpus level, 17% of reviewer-paper instances contain no panel-coded calibration, and the panel-coded calibration share is nearly $3\times$ as high in Strengths as in Weaknesses. This boundary informs three affordances: a review guideline that operationalizes the assessment-then-calibration workflow for reviewers, a per-comment rebuttal strategy scaffold for authors, and a discussion-phase dashboard for area chairs.

entry.title: The Male Abstraction Bias in Internet Culture and Large Language Models
entry.summary: Conceptual abstraction and gender are two equally central aspects of the human mind, yet they have traditionally been studied in isolation from one another, as though they were fundamentally separate. Here, we find gender and abstraction are systematically linked throughout the space of concepts spanning single (N = 40,000) and multi-word expressions (N = 67,000): across billions of words and millions of images on the internet --- and across numerous measurement techniques, including human and AI classifications --- more abstract concepts are more associated with men, a pattern we show replicates in languages around the world. This male abstraction bias not only holds across semantic domains, but it also maps onto grammatical structure: verbs and adverbs are more abstract and more male-coded, revealing a system-wide trace of stereotypes accentuating agentic qualities in men. Furthermore, we show this bias readily emerges in the free associations humans and AIs produce in controlled online tasks, indicating its psychological internalization and its algorithmic reproduction. These findings identify a latent structure in conceptual space that unifies a range of stereotypes: for example, framings of women as more embodied, emotional, and warm, versus men as more cognitive, rational, and competent; as well as erroneous views of men as better at mathematics, science, and engineering. More broadly, by analyzing an unprecedentedly large, multimodal sample of online data, we provide culture-wide evidence of gender as a core organizing principle shaping conceptual space far beyond the characterization of people and social roles.

entry.title: Contextual Pictograms for Repairing Multilingual ASR Errors
entry.summary: Speech transcription errors can be difficult to recognize when competing word hypotheses are unfamiliar or visually similar. We describe an interface that combines alternative transcripts, replay and contextually checked pictograms for selected uncertain concepts. The system will initially support French and Spanish functional utterances. A counterbalanced study will assess whether pictorial feedback helps listeners recover the speaker's intended action beyond text alternatives alone. We will also quantify semantic mismatch and additional interaction time, since an inappropriate image can reinforce the wrong interpretation rather than repair it.

entry.title: Compiling, Validating, and Using Human Reference Atlas Cell Type Annotation Crosswalks
entry.summary: The Human Reference Atlas (HRA) v2.5 includes 4,807 anatomical structures, 1,347 cell types, and 2,215 biomarkers (genes, proteins, lipids); 81 organs with 1,392 anatomical structures modeled in three dimensions (3D). Mapping new data into the HRA requires 3D spatial registration and/or cell type annotation (CTann). Many CTann tools exist but few use cell type names linked to Cell Ontology (CL), making comparisons across tools, tissues, and organs difficult. The HRA supports five transcriptomics CTann tools (Azimuth, CellTypist, popV, FR-Match, Pan-Human Azimuth), four sc-proteomics CTann tools (DeepCell Types, DeepCell Types-HuBMAP, Robust Image-Based Cell Annotator [RIBCA], and SpaTial cELl LeARning [STELLAR]), plus a Cell Distance Explorer (CDE) Spatial Omics collection covering previously published annotations across 12 tissue types with 47,349,496 cells. Assigned cell types differ in number, resolution, and coverage. This paper details how 10 crosswalks were constructed, validated, and used to compile a "Supertree" that can be used to compare CTann across organs and technologies in support of reference atlas constitution and usage. All data and code can be accessed at https://cns-iu.github.io/hra-ctann-supporting-information.

entry.title: MetamorphX: An Ungrounded 3-DoF Moment Display that Changes its Physical Properties through Rotational Impedance Control
entry.summary: Humans can estimate the properties of wielded objects (e.g., inertia and viscosity) using the force applied to the hand. We focused on this mechanism and aimed to represent the properties of wielded objects by dynamically changing the force applied to the hand. We propose MetamorphX, which uses control moment gyroscopes (CMGs) to generate ungrounded, 3-degrees of freedom moment feedback. The high-response moments obtained from CMGs allow the inertia and viscosity of motion to be set to the desired values via impedance control. A technical evaluation indicated that our device can generate a moment with a 60-ms delay. The inertia and viscosity of motion were varied by $0.01\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2}$ and $0.1\,\mathrm{N\,s}$, respectively. Additionally, we demonstrated that our device can dynamically change the inertia and viscosity of motion through virtual reality applications.
entry.arxiv:comment: 14 pages, 15 main-text figures and 8 appendix figures. Author-prepared version of the paper published at UIST 2022
entry.arxiv:journal_ref: Proceedings of the 35th Annual ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST '22), Article 72, 1-14 (2022)

entry.title: IMUdrape: Generating Garment-Mounted Virtual IMU Data from Text through Physics-Based Cloth Simulation
entry.summary: Inertial sensors are moving into clothing, from sensorized sportswear to garments instrumented with hundreds of IMUs. Sewn into clothing, a sensor no longer moves rigidly with the body: loose fabric slides, twists and swings, so a garment-mounted sensor records the motion of the fabric as well as that of the body, and this extra motion differs from one garment to the next. Models for such sensors need training data recorded with the deployed garment, yet labeled data are scarce. Virtual IMU data generated from videos or text have eased this scarcity for body-attached sensors, but existing generators attach their virtual sensors rigidly to the body. We present IMUdrape, which generates garment-mounted virtual IMU data from text through physics-based cloth simulation. IMUdrape synthesizes motion from activity descriptions, reconstructs the target garment as a sewing pattern from photographs, places virtual IMUs at the deployment's real sensor positions, and simulates the garment with an intersection-free contact solver, so that every simulation yields paired garment and body signals. On four real datasets with clothing-mounted sensors, IMUdrape improves on existing virtual-data approaches for both activity recognition and full-body pose estimation. With one real subject, its data improve recognition macro-F1 by 7% to 46% over real data alone and by 2% to 11% over body-mounted virtual data from the same motion. When the garment is simulated on recorded motion, the pose error without any real training data falls by 30% to 33% relative to generated motion, and garment data remain 12% more accurate than body data. IMUdrape thus reduces the amount of real data that garment-mounted sensing requires.
entry.arxiv:comment: 34 pages, 7 figures, 15 tables. Under review. Project page: https://zikangleng.github.io/imudrape/

entry.title: Mediating Human-Swarm Interactions Through a Robot Helper: A Shepherding-Inspired Approach
entry.summary: This work investigates human-swarm interaction (HSI) for steering large collectives through an intermediary robot helper. While prior robot-swarm control and HSI techniques commonly assume swarm members are addressable, these assumptions often fail for ``ungovernable'' swarms such as wildlife flocks and schools of fish. Motivated by pastoral shepherding, we compare low-level teleoperation to a higher-autonomy motion-primitives interface in a virtual reality (VR) shepherding task under varied swarm cohesion dynamics. Results indicate that motion primitives that operate on collective shape (e.g., boundary-based control) improve task performance and reduce perceived workload.

entry.title: Creating Hybrid Interactive Narrative Systems with LLM: From Formal Description to Evaluation
entry.summary: Interactive narratives let users shape a story while an Experience Manager (EM) keeps it coherent, balancing player freedom against authorial control. Large Language Models now enable a new generation of hybrid EMs, which combine run-time generation from free-text input with symbolic narrative control. However, their heterogeneity makes them hard to compare: A manager's behaviour is generally tied to the unique and specific scenario in which it operates, and much of its decision-making takes place outside of any explicit and verifiable structure. We address this with an LLM-based narrative platform whose managers are interchangeable modules operating over a shared symbolic world model of facts, operations, and goals. Because every applied operation carries explicit preconditions and effects, each session can be analysed as a plan through a common state-transition representation and evaluated, independently of how the manager works internally, with shared indicators of four properties: player agency, EM controllability, author intent, and robustness. We implement three contrasting managers, based respectively on open generation, Monte Carlo repair, and autonomous characters, and compare them through functional analysis on an interactive Little Red Riding Hood scenario. The results show that no manager dominates on every property, giving authors and EM designers a concrete basis to select a manager according to their priorities.
entry.arxiv:journal_ref: 38th IEEE International Conference on Tools with Artificial Intelligence (ICTAI 2026), IEEE Computer Society, Nov 2026, Boca Raton, United States

entry.title: Analysing the Narrative Paradox through Formal Models and Properties in Interactive Narrative
entry.summary: Interactive narratives aim to let players influence the unfolding of a story while preserving a coherent and satisfying narrative progression. This creates a central tension, commonly described as the narrative paradox, between player autonomy and narrative control. Experience Managers (EMs) manage the story by determining how the narrative progresses in response to player behaviour. Although this paradox is widely discussed, it is rarely modelled in a way that supports systematic analysis, simulation, and comparison across management strategies. This paper proposes a formal framework for modelling and analysing the narrative paradox as a trade-off between interdependent properties shaped by EM decisions. We represent interactive narrative behaviour through an extended state-transition system in which world states are connected by player actions and system events. From this model, we formalize key properties involved in the paradox such as the player agency, EM controllability, author intent, and robustness, and define quantitative indicators derived from simulated plans. These indicators make it possible to compare EM strategies according to their ability to balance freedom, control, and narrative satisfaction. A case study compares different EM policies, showing how simulations can reveal correlations and conflicts between properties and identify compromise zones in the design space. This work contributes a reusable modelling and analysis framework for studying the narrative paradox and evaluating heterogeneous interactive narratives on shared formal grounds, with a focus on supporting the comparison and testing of EM strategies.
entry.arxiv:journal_ref: 19th International Conference on Interactive Digital Storytelling (ICIDS 2026), ARDIN (Association for Research in Digital Interactive Narratives), Nov 2026, Bangkok, France

entry.title: Making Smell Actionable in Design: Lexicon, Movement Patterns, and Gesture Cards
entry.summary: Smell is powerful in design, yet it often remains vague and difficult to work with in studios and classrooms. While olfactory HCI has produced devices, toolkits, and scenario-based applications, designers still lack teachable, shareable resources that link smell to bodily action. This paper presents a three-phase research program that makes smell actionable by moving from lived smell experiences to movement patterns and, finally, to gesture resources. We study olfactory-motor mappings and package the results as teachable design representations through a progressively narrowing method: (1) extracting smell-verb-intent relations from user narratives; (2) capturing and clustering embodied enactments into standardized upper-limb trajectory families; and (3) translating these trajectories into gesture card representations for design teaching and ideation through design workshops. We present a three-phase translational framework and empirically derived smell-gesture correspondences that structure the smell-intent-trajectory-gesture pathway, together with reusable assets (lexicon, trajectory atlas, gesture tables, and cards) that support teaching, reuse, and adaptation across contexts.

entry.title: Palimpsestic Accountability in the US Federal AI Inventories
entry.summary: An AI inventory is a structured, often public record in which a government or organization lists and describes the AI systems it uses or plans to use. Studies of single AI inventory releases describe what systems do but say little about how they are governed over time. We linked entries across three releases of the US Federal AI Use Case Inventory (2023--2025), compared answers only where both releases required them, and analyzed governance accounts through a dual deductive-inductive approach, guided by the Algorithmic Decision-Making Adapted for the Public Sector (ADMAPS) framework. As the inventory grew from 710 to 3,611 entries from 2023 to 2025, fewer required answers were left blank, but accountability was rewritten through three mechanisms. Each release \emph{redrew} the scope of the questions; agency-assigned classifications \emph{gated} what was reported; and answers were also \emph{overwritten}, with gains and losses concentrated in single agencies and little account of human oversight and judgment. These findings show that each release redraws the boundary of accountability and leaves the public to \emph{re-stitch} the records, a condition we term \textbf{palimpsestic accountability}. We recommend versioned records, reasons for every reclassification, public files that distinguish kinds of missing answers, and oversight documented as conditions to improve public sector AI accountability.

entry.title: Just the Facts: How Dialogues with AI Reduce Conspiracy Beliefs
entry.summary: Personalized dialogues with AI substantially reduce conspiracy beliefs. To identify why, we conducted two experiments with U.S. adults recruited online (total N = 2,193) that removed possible causes one at a time. The debunking effect was robust to disclosing the AI's persuasive goal, framing the exchange as a debate, instructing the AI to inform rather than persuade, halving its response length, altering how beliefs were measured, and replacing the dialogue with a single tailored message. Only instructing the AI to persuade without factual evidence and arguments substantially reduced the debunking effect. Content analyses of the AI's output and participants' own accounts linked larger reductions in conspiracy beliefs to factual argumentation rather than rapport, storytelling, or appeals to empathy. AI dialogues appear to reduce conspiracy beliefs primarily by supplying relevant, well-reasoned counterevidence. Our results suggest that humans might be similarly effective if they could supply comparable evidence.

entry.title: Haptic Shared Control for Multi-Robot Systems
entry.summary: Multi-agent systems offer significant advantages in terms of flexibility and redundancy, enabling the efficient distribution of complex tasks among multiple robots. However, their deployment requires advanced control strategies to ensure optimal cooperation between autonomous agents and human operators. We propose a modification of the global connectivity maintenance algorithm to incorporate measurements taken in agent's local frame, using sensors with limited fields of view. This algorithm, responsible for the autonomous behavior of the multi-robot system, is combined with different adaptive supervision strategies, allowing the user to exert control at varying scales over the entire group. (i) Single Agent Control (S): The operator directly controls a single robot, (ii) Pinning Control (P): The operator imposes constraints on multiple robots to influence the group, (iii) Centroid Control (C): The operator acts on the system's center of mass to steer the entire fleet. In conjunction with the connectivity maintenance algorithm, these methods ensure compliance with inter-agent constraints while providing haptic feedback to the user regarding the system's connectivity state. The effectiveness of these approaches was evaluated through a user study, comparing performance with and without haptic feedback across multiple scenarios tailored to the different control modes.
entry.arxiv:comment: PhD thesis, Université de Rennes (IRISA UMR 6074 / Inria Rennes), defended 30 April 2025. 134 pages, 38 figures

entry.title: Who is the Pronoun Pro? Comparing LLMs and Humans at Number-Disambiguation of 'they'
entry.summary: This study evaluates whether large language models (LLMs) can reliably replace or complement human research assistants in linguistically complex annotation. In a controlled annotation task, 73 human annotators (local students and crowdworkers with and without a background in linguistics) and more than 40 LLM configurations number-disambiguated 174 authentic uses of 'they' from Reddit, including innovative and context-sensitive cases. The best LLM, Kimi K3, reached 94.5% accuracy, above the human majority vote (86.2%) and the mean of the top half of human annotators (78.5%); only the single best human annotator scored higher (95.7%). LLMs also offer substantial practical advantages in cost and speed. However, qualitative error analysis reveals a crucial complementarity: human reasoning in low-agreement cases exposes inconsistencies in the annotation typology and thereby improves the methodological framework itself. The study contributes (i) a benchmark-style human-LLM comparison for a semantically demanding task, (ii) transparent cost and time evidence, and (iii) a methodological argument against a purely replacement-oriented view of automation. LLMs are viable for large-scale annotation support in linguistics, but their responsible use requires human critical oversight. The dataset with its gold-standard labels, all human and LLM annotations, and the fully reproducible code are openly available as a Quarto-based, public repository.
entry.arxiv:comment: Submitted to journal for publication, will be updated upon publication; figures are greyscale-compatible; raw data, fully reproducible code, and Quarto source in linked repository

entry.title: False Reassurance in LLM Severe-Weather Guidance: A Replayable Evaluation Against Real NWS Alerts
entry.summary: An LLM assistant that cannot see official severe-weather alerts may tell users that conditions are calm while a warning is active. We call this false reassurance and measure it by replaying 117 frozen cases built from real U.S. National Weather Service (NWS) alerts (69 alert cases, 32 no-alert controls, 16 non-U.S. locations) through five conditions of a Claude-based preparedness pipeline that differ in alert access and prompt design. One rater hand-labeled all 342 alert-case responses under a seven-category scheme written after an initial binary pass, which we disclose. False reassurance was 0.0% for the production pipeline (0/66, 95% CI 0.0-5.5) and for the same alerts under a neutral prompt (0/69), 37.7% for a blind neutral prompt (26/69), and 44.9% when the blind prompt also told the model to disclose its blind spot (31/69). Every case was implicit; no response explicitly denied an alert. Real alerts removed false reassurance (paired McNemar p < 0.0001); the disclosure instruction did not (p = 0.40). An automated regex measure suggested the opposite and missed 53 of 57 true cases, so we do not use it. Alert data alone was not enough for safe behavior: with a neutral prompt the model raised some alarm on 87.5% of no-alert controls, against 0% under the production prompt, and a preregistered single-sentence ablation showed that one production instruction explains part of that gap. We also report two failures common to similar systems, NWS test products ingested as real alerts and a token budget that fails on complex cases, and we release the dataset, labels and code.
entry.arxiv:comment: 7 pages, 3 tables. Dataset and code: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23901549

entry.title: Spatial Organization Is Accessibility Structure: Hierarchical Screen Reading of Mobile UIs
entry.summary: Screen readers for blind and low-vision (BLV) users flatten mobile UIs into a linear sequence. Modern mobile UIs, however, contain dozens of elements grouped by spatial layout. Such linear access is ill-suited for BLV users, who must infer each element's meaning and which elements form a functional unit. Drawing on a quantitative TalkBack audit and formative interviews, we present Spatial Screen Reader (SeeR), which builds a function-aware hierarchy from accessibility metadata and provides unit summaries with hierarchical navigation. Compared with TalkBack, SeeR reduces non-informative focus stops by 82.1% and navigation steps by 52.7%. With ten BLV participants, summaries helped them connect controls to their functions and skip nonessential elements, especially on unfamiliar pages, though extra navigation levels added effort when the target was already known. These findings recast spatial organization as accessibility information: apps and platforms should expose it, rather than leaving screen readers to infer it post hoc.

entry.title: Go-Go-Go: the game of Go without turns
entry.summary: The study of variants of classic games has a long history, with chess alone inspiring countless variants that have been proposed, analyzed, and studied. The game of Go, despite rivaling chess in age, cultural relevance, popularity, and strategic depth, has seen drastically fewer variants. We introduce Go-Go-Go, a variant of the classic game of Go where there are no turns, and players play stones simultaneously and asynchronously on the board. The variant (which is to be played through a computer) includes a basic mechanism to avoid excessive spamming of moves, by imposing a minimal delay between moves that depends on their relative spatial distance. Apart from the lack of time discretization, most of the ruleset of the original game is either directly maintained or adapted in a natural way that preserves the original spirit. The first playtesting indicates that this results in the preservation of much of the emerging strategies and "flavor" of Go, while replacing the long strategic reasoning with fast paced, instinctive action fueled by quick reflexes. Play testers also report the need to balance immediate but suboptimal reactions with more reasoned but slower plays. We offer a publicly available, playable, OpenSource, and online reference implementation of Go-Go-Go at http://gogogo.di.unimi.it

entry.title: You Know What You Will Like: People Predict Their Own Ratings Better Than Recommender Systems
entry.summary: Recommender systems usually learn what people want from what they have done. Platforms could also ask people directly, but asking is costly: 98.8% of the prompts in our data went unanswered. Theories of statistical prediction imply that a person's own forecast adds little to a recommender algorithm built from many people's behavior. Theories of dispersed knowledge imply that people hold information about their own taste that the data lack. We test the two with the MovieLens Beliefs dataset. In 2023-2024, a homepage prompt asked members how they expected to rate movies they said they had not seen. Of 26,020 such expectations, 551 from 277 members were followed by a rating at least a day later. We compare each expectation with four benchmarks: the platform's own predicted rating, two collaborative-filtering models (matrix factorization and an item neighborhood), and a stack trained on other members' outcomes. The trained models use each member's latest ratings. People predict their own ratings more accurately than all four benchmarks (correlation 0.69, against 0.34 for MovieLens and 0.54 to 0.59 for the trained recommenders). Added to all the machine forecasts and features, the expectation lowers out-of-sample mean squared error by 26%. The gain holds when models are trained on earlier expectations and tested on later ones. A member's earlier expectations about other movies do not replace the current one. In ordering a member's own movies, the trained recommenders are statistically indistinguishable from the person. On old, heavily rated movies, the machines do as well or better. The results reconcile the two theories: the crowd's data suffice where they are rich, and the person adds information about the specific item. We derive four design principles for preference elicitation and recommender evaluation.

entry.title: Sure Enough to Share? Overconfidence in GenAI Video Discernment is Associated with Sharing Intentions
entry.summary: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is blurring the line between synthesized and recorded videos, but less is known about people's awareness of their discernment abilities and the consequences of miscalibration. This study examines three forms of overconfidence in GenAI video discernment (i.e., overestimation, overplacement, and overprecision) and their associations with source judgments and sharing intentions in an online study (N = 973). Participants evaluated videos depicting everyday scenes and achieved 62.5% accuracy. Three forms of overconfidence showed distinct patterns: participants overplaced themselves by 12.8 percentile points, but overprecision showed consistent positive associations with sharing intentions and the tendency to classify videos as human-made. Age, GenAI usage, and AI literacy showed consistent positive associations with all three forms of overconfidence. These findings highlight the importance of distinguishing the three forms of overconfidence to better understand GenAI engagement and incorporating metacognition into interventions to support informed media consumption.

entry.title: BobFlow: Towards Human-Agent Collaborative Data Science Using Dataflows
entry.summary: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have established human-agent collaboration as a promising paradigm for data science. Effective collaboration requires a shared computational abstraction that enables agents to reason about processing logic while allowing human analysts to understand, guide, and refine the analysis. Although scripts written in Python or SQL provide precise control, their syntax and execution details can be difficult for analysts to understand and modify. In this paper, we argue that dataflows are an effective abstraction for human-agent collaboration in data science. We introduce BobFlow, a system that combines the dataflow abstraction with the ReAct paradigm. It enables agents to iteratively construct and execute dataflows for data science tasks while allowing analysts to inspect the analysis and provide feedback. Our user study shows that BobFlow helps analysts understand, inspect, and verify agent-generated analyses. A thorough experimental evaluation across proprietary and open-weight LLMs shows accuracy score gains of up to 18.6 points at just over 1/3 of a script-based ReAct agent's inference cost.

entry.title: Digital Security Under Compound Threats: Surveillance, Threat Reasoning, and Habituation Among North Korean Defectors in China
entry.summary: North Korean defectors residing in China face persistent uncertainty regarding digital security and privacy. Through semi-structured interviews with 19 defectors, we examine how individuals understand digital threats and adapt their security behaviors. We identify three interrelated conditions: transnational surveillance pressure from North Korea, identity-linked digital infrastructure and intermediary dependency in China, and threat reasoning shaped by prior surveillance schemas. Participants developed uneven protective practices and followed two trajectories: adaptive habituation driven by knowledge acquisition and erosive habituation driven by the prolonged absence of adverse events. Our findings show how compound threats, attribution uncertainty, and constrained agency shape security reasoning among undocumented users.
entry.arxiv:comment: Accepted by IEEE S&P 27, Lionel Z. Wang is the corresponding author

entry.title: VREgo: Consumer VR Headsets for Learning Robot Manipulation from Egocentric Demonstrations
entry.summary: VREgo trains manipulation policies from demonstrations recorded on consumer VR headsets; we instantiate it with EgoKit on one such headset, the PICO 4 Ultra. On-device head and hand tracking and stereo object localisation allow the operator to begin a demonstration at the table. We adapt HumanEgo's preprocessing to estimate grasp thresholds per recording, update object positions after release, and propagate segmentation masks between keyframes. We evaluate policies in simulation on two tabletop tasks recorded by one operator. For cube placement, we compare PICO and Project Aria recordings of the same 41 layouts. With 40 training demonstrations, the PICO policies placed the cube on the tray in 67, 74, and 60 of 100 evaluation layouts across three training seeds. The corresponding Aria results were 73, 78, and 0. For a two-stage stacking task recorded with the PICO alone, the baseline placed the block on the tray in 94 of 100 layouts and met the end-of-episode criterion for both placements in two. In one diagnostic episode, repeated replanning deferred release beyond the eight executed steps. Demonstration replays also showed that the open gripper could displace the cube before grasping it. After adapting the training trajectories and adding task-specific execution rules that use simulator object positions, the system met both placement criteria in 93.8% of episodes across four evaluation noise seeds. The same 100 layouts informed rule development and evaluation. VREgo is available at https://vrego.chuange.org/.

entry.title: Tasteply: Externalizing Stable and Situational Preference as Manipulable Spatial Objects
entry.summary: Most recommender systems treat user preferences as a single signal to infer and optimize, yet human preferences are a mix of a stable preference and situational preferences that turn on and off depending on context. Through Tasteply, we externalize this preference structure as manipulable spatial objects. Tasteply represents each situational preference as an attractor and the stable preference as an underlying global field. Users can adjust their feed by moving around the space and adjusting the strength of the global field, turning the preference structure that remains latent within the model into something they can see and act on directly to steer the recommendation algorithm. Through an exploratory study (N=5), we found that this spatial control was effective, along with its limits and future direction as a means of manipulating preference-based recommendations.

entry.title: Entering a New Domain in the Era of Generative AI: An Autoethnography of Solo Game Development as a Bioinformatics Educator
entry.summary: The rapid improvement of generative AI (GenAI) not only increased the efficiency of practice but also empowered individuals with capabilities to explore new domains. However, identity formation in the wake of such empowerment remains understudied. We use an autoethnography to understand identity formation in the context of solo game development as a bioinformatics educator. With the goal of developing a create-your-own-adventure (CYOA) game, we collected data for 73 days through journal entries, interacting with communities of practices. The autoethnographer had continuously reassessed the situation, and closely interacted with communities of practice. Their prior knowledge was used to provide in-game context and to uniquely interpret game development processes. These findings suggest that the autoethnographer made efforts to belong to communities of practice and engaged extensively in sensemaking through the lens of a bioinformatics educator. Although GenAI puts power at hand, attaining a new identity took place at a human pace.

entry.title: What to Delegate, What to Preserve: Human Preferences for Agentic AI Across Everyday Life and Work
entry.summary: AI agents can execute multi-step tasks on users' behalf, yet the boundaries of acceptable delegation remain unclear. We report a scenario-based survey of 289 U.S. adults with prior AI experience covering 45 use cases across nine life domains. Each respondent evaluated one scenario per domain, producing repeated measures of automation preference, trust, collaboration, AI leadership, privacy concern, and willingness to pay. Automation preferences varied substantially across domains. Generalized estimating equation models showed that greater trust in the AI agent, desired AI leadership, prior task-specific AI use, and anticipated financial savings were associated with greater automation preference. In contrast, concerns that automation would reduce personal fulfillment predicted lower automation preference. Open-ended responses further revealed a preference for bounded autonomy, with participants often favoring substantial AI execution while retaining human involvement, oversight, or final authority. We argue that delegation is best understood as a configuration of execution, collaboration, leadership, and authority.

entry.title: "A Space Where I Can Be Myself": Exploring Safe Visibility for Graduate Student Mothers in Mom Cafes
entry.summary: Graduate student mothers navigate intertwined demands of graduate study and caregiving, yet little is known about how they seek support through online communities. We examine this through Mom Cafes, locally based online parenting communities in South Korea. Drawing on focus group interviews and design workshops with 22 graduate student mothers, we identify a pattern of dual invisibility: caregiving circumstances were difficult to make legible in academic contexts, while academic circumstances were difficult to make legible in parenting contexts. Although Mom Cafes offered useful local information and emotional reassurance, concerns specific to graduate student motherhood were harder to articulate or safely disclose. Participants sought ways to make graduate student motherhood recognizable when relevant, but their designs highlighted tensions around identifiability, judgment, relational burden and accountability. We conceptualize these tensions as safe visibility and discuss infrastructures for selective recognition, low-obligation connection, and accountable pathways to practical care.
entry.arxiv:comment: 28 pages, 1 table; 1 table and 3 figures in appendix

entry.title: Driver Takeovers and Longitudinal Responses Analysis from Naturalistic Driving
entry.summary: As Level 2 advanced driver-assistance systems (ADAS) become more widely used, understanding driver-system interaction is increasingly important for traffic safety. However, limited real-world data make these interactions difficult to study. We present ADAS-TO, a naturalistic dataset of 16,446 takeover clips from 364 drivers across 2,585 different drives. It combines road video, vehicle kinematics, driver inputs, and ADAS status. To analyze takeover behavior, we retained 6,206 manually reviewed takeover events during continued lane keeping or car following. We excluded events in which the driver intentionally changed lanes, turned, or made a stop beyond the ADAS's capabilities (e.g., at a red light or stop sign) shortly after takeover. Drivers began intervening before ADAS disengaged in 65.6% of takeovers involving braking or steering. When the ego vehicle was still closing on a lead vehicle at disengagement, longitudinal safety margins often narrowed further after the transfer to manual control. Among 2,031 such events, 78.5% had a lower minimum time-to-collision (TTC) in the five seconds after disengagement than in the five seconds before it. For events involving braking, the mean TTC trajectory reached its minimum about 1.2 s after disengagement. We model the subsequent braking response using a Gazis-Herman-Rothery (GHR) car-following law. Its median five-second spacing root-mean-square error is 1.34 m with observed lead motion and 1.84 m with predicted lead motion. The fitted model expresses braking as a response to looming, with stronger responses at higher speeds and shorter gaps. Applied before takeover, it shows that greater looming than predicted by the human-response reference is associated with disengagement. These findings support continued assessment of longitudinal safety after ADAS disengagement, while the driver's braking response develops.
entry.arxiv:comment: 28 pages, 14 figures. See arXiv:2603.06986 for the companion dataset paper. The longitudinal subset is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/HenryYHW/ADAS-TO_longitudinal

entry.title: Rhythmic Fitness Beat 'Em All using Real-Time Monocular Human Pose Estimation
entry.summary: Short and frequent physical activity exercices mitigate the health risks of sedentary behavior. Yet, the lack of motivation remains a critical barrier to adoption. Exergames gamify physical activity, but most rely on dedicated hardware, and outside dance and rhythm games they rarely use the musical beat. We present a work-in-progress beat 'em up exergame played with the whole body in front of a single smartphone, which runs the entire pipeline: an off-the-shelf real-time 3D human mesh recovery model on the phone's neural processing unit, gesture recognition, and the game, shown on any TV through a USB-C to HDMI cable. Our contributions are (1) a 3D recognition of five shadow-boxing moves (guard, punch, slip, squat, jump), each defined by one metric measure in a body frame aligned with gravity and one threshold with hysteresis, personalised during a tutorial; (2) a rhythm stage whose discrete cues are placed on the song's kick drum and judged on the movement's capture time, with a delay learned for each player; and (3) a phone-only architecture, running at 30 frames per second, that turns a phone and an HDMI cable into an exergame console.

entry.title: RAG-Enhanced LLMs for Interactive Explainability in Clinical Decision Support Systems
entry.summary: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in high-risks decision-making systems across domains such as healthcare, finance, and the judicial system. As reliance on predictive models grows, so does the demand for Explainable AI (XAI) to ensure transparency, trust, and interpretability. However, existing XAI approaches often fail to present explanations in a format accessible to domain experts, limiting their practical utility. Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently emerged as a bridge between complex models and end-users, offering natural language explanations. Yet, their use introduces new risks, including hallucinated outputs and lack of source traceability. To address these challenges, we propose a Clinical Decision Support System (CDSS) that not only combines standard predictive models with XAI techniques but also incorporates a Retrieval-Augmented Generation module as an interactive enhancer. This module grounds explanations in verified medical knowledge, reformulates technical outputs into a human-like format, and enables users-such as clinicians-to actively query the system. By fostering an interactive, human-in-the-loop environment, our approach empowers domain experts to explore model decisions, contextualize explanations, and build trust in AI-assisted diagnostics. The study concludes with preliminary experiments validating the proposed methodology.

entry.title: Interface Quilt: Modifying Applications with Computer Use Agents and Generative UI
entry.summary: Modifying an existing application is difficult when it does not provide programmatic access for that change. Recent advances in computer-use agents (CUAs) enable richer understanding and operation of existing interfaces, while generative UI (GenUI) makes it practical to generate new ones. We examine how these advances expand software modification through a design space of what can be changed and a framework for how modifications can be implemented. We then introduce Interface Quilt, a system that combines CUAs and GenUI to generate interface patches, which are new interfaces displayed over an existing application to modify its presentation, interaction, and capabilities. Through demonstrations across a variety of applications, we show that interface patches support a range of modifications without source code, APIs, or accessibility data.

entry.title: User Engagement in Visualization: A Scoping Review of 243 Research Articles
entry.summary: User engagement is well studied in other domains. Work to date has proposed conceptual models and definitions, approaches to measurement, and factors that influence engagement in digital interactions. However, of the articles in the visualization literature that refer to engagement, few of them make evidence-based, generalizable claims, and research that does is challenging to locate due to inconsistent reporting and often lacks connection to the broader engagement literature. To address these issues and promote the consideration of the broader engagement literature, we conduct a comprehensive scoping review of visualization literature and engagement. Using scoping review methodology, we identify and analyze 243 articles that make claims about engagement with visualizations. We coded the studies conducted, literature cited, definitions provided, and claims made in these articles and analyze the codes to evaluate the quality of the work in the field and to synthesize existing findings. We find that, despite frequent references to engagement and apparent interest in the topic, the overall quality of visualization engagement research is poor, often with weak evidence, inconsistent conceptualizations, and infrequent citation of existing models, methods, or claims. We report the evidence-based claims about what engages people with visualization, including the factors of animation, interaction, and immersion, additionally describing both corroboration and apparent contradictions between these claims. Finally, we propose the COMFI framework and mnemonic for reporting important information in future engagement studies.

entry.title: Harassment on TikTok: A Mixed-Methods Analysis of Video Content and Psycholinguistic Comment Stances
entry.summary: Despite extensive research on harassment, how it manifests on short--form video platforms such as TikTok---and how it shapes user interactions---remains underexplored, though these dynamics are critical for designing effective safety strategies for online communities. We present a mixed-methods study of 190 TikTok videos tagged with hashtag harassment and their 66,337 comments. Our qualitative analysis of videos identifies harassment types (sexual, verbal, stalking, law enforcement, bullying, catcalling, and gaslighting) and their characteristics (e.g., location, target, video style, and theme), along with engagement patterns. Although sexual harassment was the most prevalent topic, it did not have the highest engagement; instead, stalking--related videos received the most views. Pairwise comparisons and regression--based analyses of comments' psycholinguistic features and stance (support, opposition, neutrality) revealed differences in emotional tone, social orientation, and cognitive categories across harassment types. Comments on sexual harassment frequently express solidarity with victims, whereas discussions of law enforcement harassment emphasize institutional critique. We provide implications of our findings, demonstrating that harassment on TikTok is multifaceted, shaped by content, context, and community norms.

entry.title: The Vibe Paradox: What EEG Reveals About Your Brain When Vibe Coding
entry.summary: Background: Much of the enthusiasm for vibe coding rests on two intuitive beliefs: (1) that developers stay invested even when they no longer write the code, and (2) that delegating more of the work to AI lowers their cognitive load. Objective: Our goal was to investigate whether developers' neurophysiological states and interactions with AI are consistent with these beliefs when they work with agentic vs. non-agentic AI on their own project vs. a legacy codebase. Method: We conducted an exploratory within-subjects crossover study with 11 participants across 22 sessions. Each participant used GitHub Copilot Chat in one session and Cursor Agents in the other, working on their own project and a legacy codebase, with tool-codebase pairings randomly assigned and session order counterbalanced. We recorded participants' EEG, on-screen activity, and prompts, and analyzed 7,924 EEG data points, 984 activities, and 141 prompts. Results: Our findings contradict both beliefs. With the agent, participants remained indifferent to task outcomes, even on their own projects, and cognitive load was higher than with non-agentic AI. Furthermore, their ways of interacting shifted: with non-agentic AI, participants asked how the code worked and read it to verify changes; with the agent, they described desired app behavior and checked results in the running app. Conclusion: Our study reveals a vibe paradox: delegating to an agent left participants motivationally disinterested, even on their own projects, without relieving cognitive load, while coinciding with increased trust in AI. The community should treat this paradox as a first-class concern if developers and their AI agents are to go far together, and not just fast.

entry.title: A dynamic backrest may help accommodate trunk movement, and multi-device work elicits more of it: An exploratory comparison of high-end office chairs under single- and multi-device tasks
entry.summary: Dynamic-sitting office chairs are usually compared with static sitting rather than with each other, and the contribution of backrest deformability (lateral backrest movement) is unknown. Office work also increasingly spans multiple devices. Twenty healthy adults (10 men, 10 women) completed a 15-minute single-device and a 15-minute multi-device proofreading task on each of three chairs: two commercial dynamic-sitting chairs (T90, Aeron) and a T90 whose backrest lateral movement was mechanically fixed (T90-fixed). We recorded subjective ratings, head and trunk posture (inertial measurement units), upper trapezius and lateral gastrocnemius activity (electromyography), and task performance. Chair effects were largely null: T90 and Aeron did not differ in ratings or performance, posture and muscle activity showed only isolated, direction-inconsistent differences, and preferences were polarized. The standard T90 showed greater trunk movement (mean absolute angular velocity in yaw) than T90-fixed during the multi-device task (p = 0.042), which may indicate that its movable backrest helps accommodate trunk movement under demanding work; no other whole-sample posture, muscle, rating or performance measure differed between these two configurations, and replication is needed. Task effects were large and consistent: the multi-device task elicited greater and faster head, trunk and shoulder movement and higher upper trapezius activity than the single-device task, with lower reading throughput. Multi-device work thus imposes substantially greater movement demands than single-device work, which supports designing chairs that accommodate movement in modern work environments.

entry.title: Adjustment control usability and dynamic accommodation in office chairs: A comparative study of two contemporary designs
entry.summary: Adjustability is a core determinant of ergonomic fit in office chairs, but its benefits depend on users being able to operate the controls and, on the chair, continuing to support the body as posture changes during work. We compared two high-end office chairs, the T90 (Sidiz; Chair A) and the Aeron (Herman Miller; Chair B), in two experiments to explore which design features may explain differences between them. In Experiment 1, 20 participants adjusted ten controls common to both chairs and rated perceived adjustment difficulty on four items. Chair A had significantly lower overall difficulty (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p = 0.008), with control-level advantages for headrest angle, armrest height, armrest rotation angle and lumbar support position; Chair B was easier for seat height, possibly because its side-mounted lever is more visible than Chair A's underside button. The headrest comparisons involved a third-party headrest fitted to Chair B, and control- and item-level tests were not corrected for multiple comparisons. In Experiment 2, the same participants completed a 15-minute multi-device task requiring repeated posture changes, reach and reorientation, then rated body-part discomfort, general comfort and satisfaction with five components. Discomfort and comfort did not differ; Chair A had higher satisfaction for the seat-pan and lumbar support (exploratory, uncorrected). Interviews suggested links to mechanism properties: Chair B's rear lumbar dial was often described as producing little perceptible change, and for controls without significant differences each chair appeared to leave a different aspect of the same need unmet. These findings suggest mechanical and interface properties that designers of adjustable office chairs may consider for dynamic, multi-device work.

entry.title: Capable but Not Scalable: Requirements and Interaction Costs of Building Multi-View CAD Datasets for Design Research
entry.summary: Transforming CAD models into consistent multi-view image datasets is increasingly important for AI-driven product design research, yet existing workflows can impose substantial burdens on researchers without programming expertise. We examine this challenge from a human-computer interaction (HCI) perspective by analyzing ten reported rendering practices and deriving fourteen requirements spanning dataset quality, visual consistency, and user interaction. We then assess eleven development- and design-oriented tools against an illustrative task involving STEP models, interpreting potential interaction costs through the cognitive dimensions framework. Our analysis reveals a gap between technical capability and practical scalability: programming-based frameworks offer flexible automation but require coding expertise, while graphical design tools provide accessible functionality yet retain repetitive per-product operations. No assessed workflow combines a low programming threshold, low repetition viscosity, and flexible protocol configuration. Based on these findings, we propose design directions including reusable rendering presets, collection-wide previews and corrections, mixed-initiative orientation assignment, and automatic provenance recording. This work reframes CAD dataset generation as an end-user interaction design problem and establishes requirements for more accessible, scalable dataset creation tools.

entry.title: Selfrionette: A Fingertip Force-Input Controller for Continuous Full-Body Avatar Manipulation and Diverse Haptic Interactions
entry.summary: We propose Selfrionette, a controller that uses fingertip force input to drive avatar movements in virtual reality (VR). This system enables users to interact with virtual objects and walk in VR using only fingertip force, overcoming physical and spatial constraints. Additionally, by fixing users' fingers, it provides users with counterforces equivalent to the applied force, allowing for diverse and wide dynamic range haptic feedback by adjusting the relationship between force input and virtual movement. To evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed method, this paper focuses on hand interaction as a first step. In User Study 1, we measured usability and embodiment during reaching tasks under Selfrionette, body tracking, and finger tracking conditions. In User Study 2, we investigated whether users could perceive haptic properties such as weight, friction, and compliance under the same conditions as User Study 1. Selfrionette was found to be comparable to body tracking in realism of haptic interaction, enabling embodied avatar experiences even in limited spatial conditions.

entry.title: OpenZilo: An Open Smart-Ring Platform for Human-Centric Sensing and Interaction with Robots
entry.summary: Wearable robot interfaces must connect user input to timely physical action. We present the proposed platform, an open smart-ring platform for studying this connection across task stages. The ring integrates a microphone, an inertial measurement unit, photoplethysmography, and skin-temperature sensing. Its software architecture separates acquisition, event interpretation, interaction policy, and robot execution. We characterize seven operating modes and evaluate speech and gesture control with 10 participants. Across five commands and 250 trials per modality, speech and gestures achieved task success rates of 90.4% and 88.8%, respectively. Recognition accuracy exceeded task success for both modalities. Gaussian hidden Markov models achieved higher accuracy than a support vector machine across three vocabulary sizes, with longer scoring times. Following a shared spoken task start, gesture-based adjustments had shorter median response times than speech. Whole-task success was 70.0% with gestures and 64.0% with speech. We further examine physiological-event-triggered robot interaction using simulated event notifications. Mean notification-receipt-to-arrival times were 11.71 s for the robot and 9.20 s for an on-site person. These descriptive findings support evaluating wearable robot interfaces through both recognition and physical outcomes, with timing measures appropriate to each task stage.

entry.title: A Study on the Effects of Finger Movements on a Humanoid Hugging Robot
entry.summary: This study aimed to examine the impact of finger movements in hugging robots on users by experimentally investigating how the presence and patterns of such movements affect users psychologically. The results suggest that the presence and patterns of finger movements influence the sensations users seek from the robot; specifically, repetitive movements and asynchronous movements across multiple fingers tended to enhance these sensations. Additionally, simultaneous movement of all fingers and gentle hugging tended to evoke a greater sense of care. Conversely, no differences were observed regarding resistance to physical contact initiated by the robot.

entry.title: Setting the Stage: Enhancing Music Recommendations with Spoken Introductions to Stimulate Serendipity
entry.summary: People like to keep their music listening fresh and interesting, but recommender systems often struggle to support this need. Even when a recommended song is potentially refreshing and enriching, listeners may not perceive it as such. Building on Silvia's appraisal theory of interest, this paper studies whether enhancing recommendations with spoken introductions, immersive or informative, can stimulate two distinct flavors of experienced serendipity: taste-broadening (sparking interest in music outside one's typical preferences) and taste-deepening (deepening interest in music within one's typical preferences). Results from a large-scale user study show that both introduction types stimulate taste-broadening and taste-deepening serendipity. Taste-broadening is most effectively stimulated through transportation (absorption in a narrative world), whereas taste-deepening is most effectively stimulated through cognitive elaboration (learning something new about the artist or the social context in which the music emerged). We discuss how these findings could be translated into practice through curated taste-broadening playlists, where both introduction types appear promising, and taste-deepening playlists, where informative introductions seem particularly effective.

entry.title: Must AI Spell It Out? Pragmatic Comprehension of Alerts in a Time-Critical Task
entry.summary: Assistive systems typically tell users everything, often spending time and attention on what a user already knows, leaving less for what happens next. People, on the other hand, leave out what they expect the listener can supply. Can people use their prior knowledge to understand an incomplete message when the speaker is a machine though? We studied this pragmatic comprehension in a monitoring task controlling users' prior knowledge and the available time to detect critical situations. In a preregistered study (N=114), we compared a pragmatic planner that reasons over a model of the listener's knowledge to decide what to say, when, and how explicitly, with a baseline specifying problems fully in onset order. Participants resolved underspecified alerts almost as reliably as fully specified ones and sooner, detected more problems, and rated the pragmatic assistant helpful more often, with no increase in reported mental demand. Our findings show that people can recover what the system left implicit and that pragmatic communication can support effective assistance under the constraints of a changing world.

entry.title: SEAM: Situated Executable Associative Memory for a Co-located Community
entry.summary: In groups, knowledge is distributed among individuals, and how it is brought together depends on social ties. Taking inspiration from how a single mind recalls and reacts to memories and current stimulus, we build a shared memory that does this for a community, prototyped as a social app, SEAM. Members post arbitrary moments; SEAM works out how fragments relate, distills knowledge about the group, and replies in a situated and associative way. Some of these memories act as instructions that can alter how the system behaves, making it programmable by its members. We deployed SEAM to 46 people in a co-located community for two weeks of open-ended use, and ran a follow-up workshop with 14. Members shared their days, interrogated the memory, and instructed it to track routines and run games; replies introduced them to people and subjects they had never encountered. SEAM points towards communities where knowledge finds people.

entry.title: A Cracked Mirror: How People Perceive Gender Performance by Large Language Models
entry.summary: How do large language models (LLMs) perform gender under zero-shot prompting, and how do people interpret those performances in conversation? Drawing on gender performativity, we examine how gendered meanings emerge through generated language, conversational context and human interpretation. In a preregistered randomised online experiment, 1,060 participants each had five short conversations with an LLM. We used minimal prompts to elicit performances from "very masculine" to "very feminine" and asked participants to rate their partner's perceived gender after each conversation. Mean ratings shifted in the direction of the prompts, but ratings at the extremes were closer to the midpoint than the prompt labels implied. When prompted to perform as "neither masculine nor feminine", the models were perceived as slightly masculine on average. Ratings varied across models and conversation topics. Women and men gave similar ratings at the extremes, but women rated the models as more masculine across the intermediate prompt levels. Participants' explanations illustrate how they drew on writing style, emotional expression and conversational interests, sometimes questioning the stereotypes behind their judgements. These findings suggest that conversational AI acts as a cracked mirror of gender norms. Models reproduce recognisable cues, and people interpret and sometimes challenge the meanings those cues carry.

entry.title: How Do Artificial Agents Make Decisions in Light of Visual Data?
entry.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) have demonstrated significant advances in reasoning with visual data, which is particularly important given that much of human knowledge is encoded visually in scientific articles and other sources. However, a gap remains in understanding how artificial agents, powered by VLMs, perceive and navigate decision-making under uncertainty in the presence of visual data. This study explores this gap by evaluating and analyzing autonomous decision-making processes. Building upon prior work in visualization literacy and decision theory, we conducted two complementary studies: one examining how agents perceive and quantify uncertainty encoded in visualizations, and another investigating how artificial agents make decisions based on visual data in the form of images. We analyzed perception accuracy and decision performance across models and visualization types. Our results show that GPT-4o demonstrates the highest accuracy in perceiving uncertainty in pie and bar charts among the tested models. For decision-making, autonomous agents showed the best alignment with rational decision theory when uncertainty was represented through circle charts, icon arrays, or text.
